individual_reviews.label: reviewer_1

review.Summary: The paper argues that progress toward 'spatial supersensing' requires moving beyond language-centric and reactive video understanding toward continuous, predictive world modeling. It proposes a four-stage hierarchy (semantic perception, streaming event cognition, implicit 3D spatial cognition, predictive world modeling), introduces a new benchmark VSI-Super with two tasks (VSR for long-horizon spatial recall and VSC for continual counting), and curates a large instruction-tuning dataset VSI-590K to train Cambrian-S models. Cambrian-S achieves large gains on VSI-Bench but still fails on VSI-Super, motivating a predictive-sensing prototype that uses latent-frame prediction error ('surprise') to drive memory management and event segmentation, improving performance on VSI-Super over strong baselines.
Strengths: The paper provides a thoughtful capability hierarchy for spatial supersensing and uses it to audit existing benchmarks, showing that many video benchmarks are solvable from captions or single frames and thus rely more on language priors than genuine visual sensing.

VSI-Super is a creative benchmark design: VSR resembles a visual needle-in-a-haystack with in-frame edited objects and sequential recall, while VSC requires continual counting across concatenated scenes; both are deliberately resistant to context-length scaling.

The curation of VSI-590K from diverse real, simulated, and pseudo-annotated sources is technically sound, and the data-source ablations are informative (annotated real videos > simulated > pseudo-annotated images).
Cambrian-S obtains a large +30% absolute improvement on VSI-Bench over prior open models without sacrificing general video understanding, and this holds across model sizes from 0.5B to 7B.

The predictive-sensing proof-of-concept is a distinctive contribution: using next-latent-frame prediction error as a surprise signal for memory compression and event segmentation yields consistent gains on VSI-Super and stable GPU memory use, outperforming Gemini-2.5-Flash and existing long-video methods.
The paper is generally well structured and includes extensive ablations, training details, and benchmark construction details in the appendices.
Weaknesses: The VSI-Super benchmark is synthetic and somewhat narrow: VSR is constructed by inserting out-of-place objects and concatenating room-tour videos, and VSC concatenates VSI-Bench clips; it is unclear how well these tasks capture real-world continuous spatial cognition or generalize beyond indoor tours.

The absolute performance of the proposed predictive-sensing system remains low (e.g., VSR around 40% and VSC around 35-40%), and the claimed superiority over Gemini-2.5-Flash is demonstrated on only these two synthetic tasks with a limited set of baselines.

The surprise threshold appears to be tuned per video duration and per method, which weakens the claim of a general, unsupervised mechanism; no analysis is provided on sensitivity to this hyperparameter or on how to set it in practice without ground-truth boundaries.

The comparison to 'streaming' models such as Gemini-Live and GPT-Realtime is limited to a figure with no detailed evaluation protocol or error bars, and these APIs may not be optimized for the exact counting task.

The paper frames 'supersensing' and 'predictive world modeling' as a paradigm shift, but the actual contribution is a lightweight MLP predictor plus heuristic memory/segmentation rules; the gap between the conceptual claims and the implemented prototype is large.

No human performance baselines are reported on VSI-Super, despite the claim that the tasks are 'easy for humans'; this makes it hard to calibrate how far models are from human-level spatial supersensing.

The VSR questions are multiple-choice with only four options, which may introduce guessing-level performance and limits the diagnostic power; the benchmark report includes chance levels but not per-question confidence or error analysis.
Questions: How sensitive are VSR and VSC results to the surprise threshold, and is it possible to set this threshold without knowing ground-truth event boundaries or video statistics?
Do the reported VSC streaming results control for the fact that the same question is asked repeatedly, possibly allowing models to accumulate answers or exploit repetition?
What is the human performance on VSI-Super, and how do the proposed methods compare to humans in terms of accuracy and robustness?
Does the predictive-sensing memory system work on more diverse, non-indoor, or real-world streaming videos, and does the LFP head generalize beyond the indoor room-tour distribution?

How much of the VSI-Super gain comes from the surprise-based memory/segmentation versus the underlying strong Cambrian-S spatial model trained on VSI-590K? A model with random or uniform segmentation would help isolate this.

Were the Gemini-2.5-Flash and other API baselines given any task-specific prompting or few-shot examples, and are their context windows actually exhausted at the stated video lengths given 1 FPS sampling?
Limitations: VSI-Super is synthetic and limited to indoor environments and concatenated room-tour clips, so its conclusions may not transfer to diverse real-world streaming scenarios.
The benchmark tasks are narrow (object recall and counting) and do not cover the full breadth of the proposed 'supersensing' hierarchy.

The predictive-sensing prototype is a proof-of-concept; the LFP head is a simple MLP and the memory/segmentation heuristics are not learned end-to-end, limiting the strength of the paradigm-shift claims.
The surprise threshold requires tuning per video duration and per task, which is not a fully autonomous mechanism.
The paper does not evaluate failure cases or provide error analysis on VSI-Super, making it difficult to understand whether failures stem from perception, memory, or reasoning.

Potential negative societal impacts are not discussed, although the work is foundational and unlikely to introduce direct harms; nonetheless, surveillance-style 'supersensing' capabilities could be a concern if developed further.

individual_reviews.label: reviewer_2

review.Summary: The paper proposes a hierarchy of spatial supersensing (semantic perception, streaming event cognition, implicit 3D spatial cognition, predictive world modeling) and argues that current video MLLM benchmarks mostly test only the early stages. It introduces VSI-Super, a two-part benchmark with long-horizon visual spatial recall (VSR) and continual visual spatial counting (VSC), designed to resist brute-force context expansion. It curates VSI-590K, a 590K-pair spatial instruction-tuning dataset from annotated real videos, simulated data, and pseudo-annotated web videos, and trains Cambrian-S (0.5B-7B), which achieves >30% absolute improvement on VSI-Bench. Despite this, Cambrian-S fails on VSI-Super, motivating a predictive sensing prototype in which a self-supervised next-latent-frame predictor uses prediction error ('surprise') for memory management and event segmentation, outperforming Gemini baselines on these tasks.
Strengths: The conceptual hierarchy of spatial supersensing is a useful organizing framework and clearly identifies gaps in current benchmarks and models.

The diagnostic analysis of existing video benchmarks (blind, single-frame, captions, multi-frame conditions) provides concrete evidence about language-prior reliance, with fine-grained and interpretable comparisons.

VSI-590K is a substantial, multi-source instruction-tuning dataset; ablations show the relative value of annotated real videos, simulated data, and pseudo-annotated images, and the benefit of mixing general video data to retain broad capabilities.

Cambrian-S achieves strong state-of-the-art results on VSI-Bench, including robustness on debiased spatial reasoning and generalization to held-out route planning, without sacrificing general video understanding.

The predictive-sensing prototype is original and the ablation against adjacent-frame similarity supports the use of prediction error as a surprise signal; it demonstrates stable GPU memory and better performance scaling than Gemini on the new benchmark.
Weaknesses: The VSI-Super benchmark is synthetic and narrow: VSR edits the same unusual object into four frames of indoor tours, and VSC concatenates VSI-Bench clips; it is unclear whether these tasks measure 'supersensing' or simply a scalable needle-in-a-haystack and counting test, and only 60/50 questions per duration limit statistical reliability.

The paper overclaims: calling a two-layer MLP next-frame predictor a 'predictive world model' and statements about 'rivaling and surpassing human visual intelligence' are not supported by the proof-of-concept experiments.

Main comparisons on VSI-Super are limited (primarily Gemini-2.5-Flash, with MovieChat/Flash-VStream only in the appendix), and the surprise-driven systems rely on thresholds and memory budgets whose tuning and sensitivity are not fully analyzed; simpler scene-cut or key-frame baselines may match the gains.

The diagnostic analysis uses a single image MLLM (Cambrian-1) and Gemini-generated captions without error bars or significance testing, and the caption condition may favor certain benchmarks depending on caption quality.

VSI-590K pseudo-annotations derive from noisy object detection, segmentation, and reconstruction, and the claim of no overlap with VSI-Bench/VSI-Super needs stronger assurance because VSI-Super is built from VSI-Bench videos sourced from the same datasets (ScanNet, ScanNet++, ARKitScenes) used in training.
Questions: How was VSI-Super validated with human annotators or inter-annotator agreement, and what are the confidence intervals for the reported accuracies given only 50-60 videos per duration?
What exactly is the MRA metric for VSC, and how are model outputs parsed and aggregated when multiple segment-level answers are combined?

Are the surprise threshold and memory budgets tuned per video or per duration, and how sensitive are the results to these hyperparameters? Could a simple scene-cut detector replace the LFP surprise signal?
Can you more rigorously rule out overlap between VSI-590K training data (ScanNet, ScanNet++, ARKitScenes) and the VSI-Bench videos used in VSI-Super, beyond relying on train/test split separation?
Does the LFP auxiliary loss or surprise-based memory help on standard long-video benchmarks beyond VSI-Super, or only on tasks where scene boundaries align with ground-truth segmentation?
Limitations: The benchmark is limited to synthetic indoor room tours with edited objects; real-world open-set spatial streams may pose different challenges.
The small number of benchmark videos/questions and the lack of a human upper-bound measurement limit the strength of conclusions.
The predictive sensing prototype is minimal; it is not a full world model and is only demonstrated on two case studies.
Pseudo-annotated frames and template-generated QA pairs may introduce noise and bias into VSI-590K.
No analysis of failure modes or negative societal impact is included; while the application is not high-risk, the broad AGI-related claims merit caution.

individual_reviews.label: reviewer_3

review.Summary: The paper argues that progress in multimodal intelligence requires a shift from reactive, task-driven systems and brute-force long context toward a broader paradigm of 'spatial supersensing,' defined as a hierarchy of semantic perception, streaming event cognition, implicit 3D spatial cognition, and predictive world modeling. To make this concrete, the authors introduce VSI-Super, a two-part benchmark (VSR for long-horizon spatial recall and VSC for continual spatial counting) that is challenging for current MLLMs. They also curate a large spatial instruction-tuning dataset VSI-590K and train Cambrian-S models, achieving state-of-the-art results on VSI-Bench while showing that these models still fail on VSI-Super. Finally, they propose a predictive sensing mechanism using a self-supervised latent-frame predictor whose prediction error drives memory management and event segmentation, and they demonstrate that this approach outperforms leading proprietary baselines on VSI-Super. Contributions include the benchmark, dataset, model family, and a proof-of-concept for predictive sensing.
Strengths: The paper provides a thorough diagnostic analysis of existing video benchmarks using controlled input manipulations (single frame, captions, blind, chance), showing that many benchmarks can be partially solved with language priors alone, and that visual-spatial benchmarks like VSI-Bench are more visually demanding.

VSI-Super introduces two new tasks that are simple for humans but challenging for current MLLMs, demonstrating that even a frontier model with 1M context tokens struggles, particularly on tasks requiring cumulative counting and long-horizon recall.

The VSI-590K dataset is a substantial resource, combining 3D-annotated real videos, simulated data, and pseudo-annotated web frames, with a careful question-type taxonomy and extensive ablations showing that real video annotations are most effective; this dataset and the Cambrian-S models are likely valuable to the community.

The paper provides strong empirical evidence that data and model scaling (up to 7B) yields large gains on standard spatial benchmarks without hurting general video understanding, and that gains transfer to a debiased version of VSI-Bench, suggesting genuine visual reasoning rather than language priors.

The predictive sensing prototype is a novel application of prediction error for memory management and event segmentation, with ablations against adjacent-frame similarity, and demonstrates stable accuracy and memory usage on long videos compared with fixed-context baselines.
Weaknesses: The VSI-Super benchmark is entirely synthetic (human-inserted objects via Gemini, concatenated room tours) and lacks real-world diversity; the paper does not provide inter-annotator agreement or quality-control statistics, and the tasks may be seen as artificial 'needle-in-haystack' variants rather than true spatial cognition.

The claim that VSI-Super is 'resistant to brute-force context expansion' is not fully justified: VSC's difficulty comes largely from cumulative counting over multiple episodes, not from context length per se, and the benchmark does not directly test world-modeling abilities (e.g., prediction or planning) as claimed.

The predictive sensing method is only a proof-of-concept; improvements on VSI-Super, while better than baselines, remain low in absolute terms (e.g., ~40% VSR, ~40% MRA on VSC), the surprise threshold and memory budgets are tuned per video length, and it is unclear whether the approach would scale or generalize to more complex spatial reasoning tasks.

The comparison on VSI-Super against proprietary baselines is limited (only Gemini-2.5-Flash and Gemini-1.5-Flash), and exact numerical results with standard error or variance are not reported; the figures show qualitative trends but not rigorous statistical analysis.

The paper is extremely long and at times overstates the paradigm shift; the 'world model' is a simple next-frame prediction head, and the connection to human cognition is mostly metaphorical. Many details are relegated to appendices, and the writing could be more concise.
Questions: How many human annotators constructed the VSR benchmark, and what instructions and quality controls were used? What is the inter-annotator agreement on object placement and order?
In VSC, when computing MRA, are the counts of objects unique instances or appearances? How is the ground truth count determined for objects that appear in multiple rooms or viewpoints?

For the surprise threshold and memory budgets, are these hyperparameters tuned separately for each video duration? If so, does this constitute test-time adaptation, and what is the sensitivity to these hyperparameters?

Does the predictive sensing approach improve performance on other established long-video benchmarks (e.g., VideoMME for long videos, LongVideoBench, or MovieChat setting), or is it specific to VSI-Super?
What is the computational overhead of the LFP head and surprise estimation in terms of training and inference time? How much extra memory does it require compared to standard video MLLM inference?
Would scaling Cambrian-S to larger models (e.g., 30B or 70B) with the same data change the conclusion that scaling is insufficient for VSI-Super?
Limitations: The benchmark is limited to indoor environments and synthetic insertions; it may not capture the diversity and unpredictability of real-world streaming video.
The dataset VSI-590K is also indoor-centric, and its pseudo-annotations from web videos may be noisy.
The predictive sensing prototype is not a full world model; it only uses frame-level latent prediction and does not model dynamics or 3D structure.
The paper does not analyze failure cases on VSI-Super in detail, so it is unclear why the method fails on longer videos.
The authors disclose that the prototype is limited in quality, scale, and generalizability, but they do not discuss potential negative societal impacts of 'supersensing' or surveillance applications.

review.Summary: The paper introduces a four-stage hierarchy for 'spatial supersensing' (semantic perception, streaming event cognition, implicit 3D spatial cognition, predictive world modeling) and argues that current video MLLMs and benchmarks focus mainly on linguistic understanding and semantic perception. It presents a diagnostic analysis of existing video benchmarks under different input conditions (blind, single frame, multiple frames, frame captions) showing that many benchmarks can be solved from language priors. To address the gap, the authors propose VSI-Super, a two-part benchmark: VSR (long-horizon recall of inserted unusual objects in up to 240-minute videos) and VSC (continual counting of objects across concatenated room tours). They then curate a large spatial instruction-tuning dataset VSI-590K and train Cambrian-S, a family of spatially grounded video MLLMs, which achieve state-of-the-art results on VSI-Bench (+30% absolute over prior models) without sacrificing general video understanding. However, Cambrian-S still fails on VSI-Super, suggesting that data scaling alone is insufficient. As a proof of concept, the paper proposes 'predictive sensing' using a self-supervised next-latent-frame prediction head; the resulting prediction error ('surprise') is used for memory compression/consolidation and event segmentation, leading to substantially better performance on VSI-Super than strong long-context baselines such as Gemini-2.5-Flash.
Strengths: The paper proposes a clear and useful conceptual hierarchy for spatial supersensing, going beyond typical video-QA benchmarks and providing a roadmap for future work.

The diagnostic analysis of existing benchmarks is thorough and insightful: using blind, single-frame, multi-frame, and caption conditions shows that many popular benchmarks are heavily solvable via language priors, strengthening the motivation for new benchmarks.

VSI-Super is a well-designed stress test that is arbitrary in length and resistant to brute-force context scaling; the two tasks target distinct capabilities (sequential recall and continual counting) and are shown to be challenging even for frontier proprietary models.

VSI-590K is a large and diverse spatial instruction-tuning dataset, with careful ablations showing the complementary contributions of annotated real videos, simulated data, and pseudo-annotated images; the resulting Cambrian-S models achieve a large +30% absolute improvement on VSI-Bench and generalize to unseen spatial question types like route planning.

The predictive sensing prototype is a conceptually novel application of prediction-error signals to memory management and event segmentation in MLLMs, and it is empirically validated with ablations (prediction error vs. adjacent-frame similarity) and comparisons against proprietary streaming models.
The paper is well organized and provides extensive appendices with implementation details, benchmark construction, dataset examples, and additional results, which would help reproduction.
Weaknesses: VSI-Super is synthetic and constructed by concatenating room-tour clips and using generative editing to insert objects; it is not clear how well performance on this benchmark transfers to real-world continuous egocentric or embodied perception, so the claim of probing 'true spatial supersensing' may be overstated.

The conclusion that 'scale alone is insufficient' is based on a single model family (Cambrian-S) and one dataset; alternative architectures, larger video encoders, or different training recipes might behave differently, and the paper does not provide a systematic scaling study on VSI-Super.

The proposed predictive sensing framework is a prototype with several hand-designed components: surprise thresholds are tuned per video duration and per benchmark, the memory system has multiple hyperparameters, and the event-segmentation agent sums segment answers, which can propagate errors; the gains over strong baselines, while positive, are still far from solving the tasks.

The VSC benchmark may have ambiguities in counting: objects can be revisited across concatenated rooms, and there is no explicit definition of how repeated sightings or the same object category across rooms should be handled; the ground-truth counting appears to be derived from VSI-Bench annotations, but the evaluation metric MRA is not fully detailed in the main text.

The diagnostic analysis uses an image-based MLLM (Cambrian-1) rather than state-of-the-art video models; while this is a reasonable design choice to isolate task demands, the conclusions about benchmark 'language priors' may not fully generalize to video-specific models with temporal reasoning capabilities.

Some claims of no data overlap are made, but VSI-590K uses training splits of ScanNet, ARKitScenes, etc., while VSI-Bench uses the same source datasets; the paper argues that validation/test splits avoid overlap, but it does not demonstrate that the generated QA templates cannot leak scene statistics or object distributions from training splits.
Questions: How is the mean relative accuracy (MRA) computed for VSC exactly, and how are repeated observations of the same object across concatenated rooms handled in the ground-truth counts?
For VSR, are the inserted objects always placed in four locations chosen by human annotators, and if so, what is the inter-annotator agreement or quality control for the benchmark labels?
In the predictive sensing experiments, are the surprise thresholds tuned on the test set or on a separate validation set, and could threshold tuning per duration inflate the reported results?

The LFP head predicts the next latent frame from the current frame representation; why was this design chosen over predicting in pixel space or using a recurrent world-model module, and how sensitive are the results to the LFP loss weighting (Table 16 shows a drop at 0.5 and 1.0)?

The paper claims VSI-Super is 'resistant to brute-force context expansion,' but Gemini-2.5-Flash still handles 60-minute videos within context; what would happen if a model with a much larger context window were used, and are there any experiments with long-context models that do not run out of context?

Would the Cambrian-S model trained on VSI-590K also improve on other 3D spatial benchmarks (e.g., OpenEQA, ScanQA) or on embodied navigation tasks, or is the improvement limited to VSI-Bench-style video QA?
Limitations: The benchmarks are synthetic and limited to indoor room tours; real-world spatial supersensing involves outdoor, dynamic, and interactive environments, which are not covered.
VSI-590K relies on template-based QA generation, which may limit the diversity and naturalness of questions compared to human-written annotations.
The predictive sensing prototype is not a full world model; it uses a shallow MLP head and simple memory consolidation, so its generalizability to richer tasks and longer horizons is uncertain.

Potential privacy and copyright concerns arise from using YouTube room-tour videos and potentially identifiable indoor environments; the paper does not discuss consent or filtering of sensitive content.
Computational costs of training the Cambrian-S family on TPU v4-512s are not quantified, which makes it harder for the community to replicate or assess the environmental impact.

individual_reviews.label: reviewer_5

review.Summary: The paper argues for a shift from reactive, task-driven MLLMs toward 'spatial supersensing', organized into four stages: semantic perception, streaming event cognition, implicit 3D spatial cognition, and predictive world modeling. It audits existing video benchmarks with diagnostic input manipulations, showing many are partly solvable from captions or language priors. To address the gap, it introduces VSI-Super with two long-horizon tasks (VSR sequential object-location recall, VSC continual object counting), curates VSI-590K, trains Cambrian-S models that achieve strong VSI-Bench results, and prototypes a predictive-sensing module based on next-latent-frame prediction whose 'surprise' signal drives memory compression and event segmentation.
Strengths: Provides a clear conceptual hierarchy (semantic perception → streaming event cognition → implicit 3D spatial cognition → predictive world modeling) that is useful for positioning video benchmarks and model capabilities.

The diagnostic study of existing benchmarks (single frame, multiple frames, captions, blind) gives concrete evidence that many video QA benchmarks rely on language priors rather than genuine visual sensing.

VSI-Super is a simple but scalable benchmark family that stresses long-horizon continual spatial reasoning and is intentionally difficult for fixed-context models; the VSC saturation plots for Gemini are revealing.

VSI-590K and the Cambrian-S training pipeline are substantial empirical contributions: Cambrian-S-7B reaches 67.5 on VSI-Bench and 59.9 on VSI-Bench-Debiased, outperforming prior open and proprietary models, with extensive ablations on data sources, base models, and training mixtures.

The predictive-sensing proof of concept (LFP surprise for memory and event segmentation) shows consistent gains over long-context baselines and maintains bounded GPU memory, and the ablations against adjacent-frame similarity support the use of prediction error over a simple appearance-change signal.
Weaknesses: The VSI-Super tasks are narrow and synthetic: VSR asks about four inserted objects in concatenated room tours, and VSC asks for cumulative counts; they do not exercise the richer 'predictive world modeling' or 'implicit 3D spatial cognition' described in the hierarchy, and no human baseline is reported to calibrate difficulty.

The 'predictive sensing' paradigm claim is overstated relative to the actual contribution: the LFP head is a two-layer MLP that predicts the next latent frame and is only used to compress or segment frames; the model does not update a world model, plan, or use predictions for inference beyond computing surprise.

Surprise thresholds appear to be tuned per duration and per method on the benchmark itself, and results are reported without error bars or significance tests, so the comparative claims (especially the 40% VSR numbers) are not yet robust.

The 'without sacrificing general capabilities' claim is only partially supported: Cambrian-S-7B trails Gemini-2.5-Flash by large margins on VideoMME (63.4 vs 81.5) and VideoMMMU (38.6 vs 79.2), so the claim should be qualified to open-source/comparable-size models.

Possible domain leakage: VSI-590K is built from the same ScanNet/ScanNet++/ARKitScenes families that underlie VSI-Bench and hence VSI-Super; although the paper states train/test splits do not overlap, the model may still benefit from shared scene statistics, which weakens the claim of generalization to unseen spatial environments.
Questions: Were surprise thresholds and other hyperparameters tuned on the VSI-Super test set? If so, how does performance change with held-out threshold selection or cross-validation?
What is human accuracy on VSR and VSC across the different durations? This is needed to support the claim that the tasks are 'easy for humans' and to calibrate the benchmark.

Could a simple scene-change detector or optical-flow-based surprise signal combined with the same memory/segmentation framework match or exceed the LFP-based results? The current ablation only compares against adjacent-frame SigLIP similarity.

How does Cambrian-S with surprise memory perform on VSI-Super videos created from scenes outside the ScanNet/ARKitScenes/ScanNet++ distribution (e.g., outdoors, dynamic scenes, or other indoor datasets)?
What is the sensitivity of VSR/VSC scores to the number of inserted objects, the number of concatenated rooms, and the choice of multiple-choice vs. open-ended questions?

Why does Cambrian-S without memory obtain only 0.6 MRA on 10-minute VSC despite strong absolute counting on VSI-Bench? Does this indicate a failure in cumulative state tracking rather than spatial perception?
Are the VSI-Super evaluation sets large enough for the reported differences (e.g., 60 VSR videos and 50 VSC questions per cell) to be statistically reliable?
Limitations: The benchmark is confined to synthetic edits and concatenated indoor room tours; it does not cover embodied interaction, dynamic scenes, or open-ended spatial reasoning, so claims about 'spatial supersensing' are not fully tested.

The predictive sensing prototype is minimal: the LFP head is trained on 1-FPS frames from the same spatial SFT data, and its surprise signal is not integrated into the model's recurrent state; there is no evidence that the model learns a predictive world model beyond frame-level prediction error.
Evaluation robustness is limited by the absence of confidence intervals, multiple seeds, human baselines, and held-out threshold tuning.

Potential negative societal impact is low but could include use of long-horizon spatial monitoring for surveillance; the paper does not discuss this. No significant immediate ethical risks are identified.

review.Summary: The paper argues that progress toward 'spatial supersensing' requires moving beyond language-centric and reactive video understanding toward continuous, predictive world modeling. It proposes a four-stage hierarchy (semantic perception, streaming event cognition, implicit 3D spatial cognition, predictive world modeling), introduces a new benchmark VSI-Super with two tasks (VSR for long-horizon spatial recall and VSC for continual counting), and curates a large instruction-tuning dataset VSI-590K to train Cambrian-S models. Cambrian-S achieves large gains on VSI-Bench but still fails on VSI-Super, motivating a predictive-sensing prototype that uses latent-frame prediction error ('surprise') to drive memory management and event segmentation, improving performance on VSI-Super over strong baselines.
Strengths: The paper provides a thoughtful capability hierarchy for spatial supersensing and uses it to audit existing benchmarks, showing that many video benchmarks are solvable from captions or single frames and thus rely more on language priors than genuine visual sensing.

VSI-Super is a creative benchmark design: VSR resembles a visual needle-in-a-haystack with in-frame edited objects and sequential recall, while VSC requires continual counting across concatenated scenes; both are deliberately resistant to context-length scaling.

The curation of VSI-590K from diverse real, simulated, and pseudo-annotated sources is technically sound, and the data-source ablations are informative (annotated real videos > simulated > pseudo-annotated images).
Cambrian-S obtains a large +30% absolute improvement on VSI-Bench over prior open models without sacrificing general video understanding, and this holds across model sizes from 0.5B to 7B.

The predictive-sensing proof-of-concept is a distinctive contribution: using next-latent-frame prediction error as a surprise signal for memory compression and event segmentation yields consistent gains on VSI-Super and stable GPU memory use, outperforming Gemini-2.5-Flash and existing long-video methods.
The paper is generally well structured and includes extensive ablations, training details, and benchmark construction details in the appendices.
Weaknesses: The VSI-Super benchmark is synthetic and somewhat narrow: VSR is constructed by inserting out-of-place objects and concatenating room-tour videos, and VSC concatenates VSI-Bench clips; it is unclear how well these tasks capture real-world continuous spatial cognition or generalize beyond indoor tours.

The absolute performance of the proposed predictive-sensing system remains low (e.g., VSR around 40% and VSC around 35-40%), and the claimed superiority over Gemini-2.5-Flash is demonstrated on only these two synthetic tasks with a limited set of baselines.

The surprise threshold appears to be tuned per video duration and per method, which weakens the claim of a general, unsupervised mechanism; no analysis is provided on sensitivity to this hyperparameter or on how to set it in practice without ground-truth boundaries.

The comparison to 'streaming' models such as Gemini-Live and GPT-Realtime is limited to a figure with no detailed evaluation protocol or error bars, and these APIs may not be optimized for the exact counting task.

The paper frames 'supersensing' and 'predictive world modeling' as a paradigm shift, but the actual contribution is a lightweight MLP predictor plus heuristic memory/segmentation rules; the gap between the conceptual claims and the implemented prototype is large.

No human performance baselines are reported on VSI-Super, despite the claim that the tasks are 'easy for humans'; this makes it hard to calibrate how far models are from human-level spatial supersensing.

The VSR questions are multiple-choice with only four options, which may introduce guessing-level performance and limits the diagnostic power; the benchmark report includes chance levels but not per-question confidence or error analysis.
Questions: How sensitive are VSR and VSC results to the surprise threshold, and is it possible to set this threshold without knowing ground-truth event boundaries or video statistics?
Do the reported VSC streaming results control for the fact that the same question is asked repeatedly, possibly allowing models to accumulate answers or exploit repetition?
What is the human performance on VSI-Super, and how do the proposed methods compare to humans in terms of accuracy and robustness?
Does the predictive-sensing memory system work on more diverse, non-indoor, or real-world streaming videos, and does the LFP head generalize beyond the indoor room-tour distribution?

How much of the VSI-Super gain comes from the surprise-based memory/segmentation versus the underlying strong Cambrian-S spatial model trained on VSI-590K? A model with random or uniform segmentation would help isolate this.

Were the Gemini-2.5-Flash and other API baselines given any task-specific prompting or few-shot examples, and are their context windows actually exhausted at the stated video lengths given 1 FPS sampling?
How is the mean relative accuracy (MRA) computed for VSC exactly, and how are repeated observations of the same object across concatenated rooms handled in the ground-truth counts?
For VSR, are the inserted objects always placed in four locations chosen by human annotators, and if so, what is the inter-annotator agreement or quality control for the benchmark labels?
In the predictive sensing experiments, are the surprise thresholds tuned on the test set or on a separate validation set, and could threshold tuning per duration inflate the reported results?

Could a simple scene-change detector or optical-flow-based surprise signal combined with the same memory/segmentation framework match or exceed the LFP-based results? The current ablation only compares against adjacent-frame SigLIP similarity.

How does Cambrian-S with surprise memory perform on VSI-Super videos created from scenes outside the ScanNet/ARKitScenes/ScanNet++ distribution (e.g., outdoors, dynamic scenes, or other indoor datasets)?

Why does Cambrian-S without memory obtain only 0.6 MRA on 10-minute VSC despite strong absolute counting on VSI-Bench? Does this indicate a failure in cumulative state tracking rather than spatial perception?
Are the VSI-Super evaluation sets large enough for the reported differences (e.g., 60 VSR videos and 50 VSC questions per cell) to be statistically reliable?
Limitations: VSI-Super is synthetic and limited to indoor environments and concatenated room-tour clips, so its conclusions may not transfer to diverse real-world streaming scenarios.

The benchmark tasks are narrow (object recall and counting) and do not cover the full breadth of the proposed 'supersensing' hierarchy, particularly predictive world modeling or implicit 3D spatial cognition.

The predictive-sensing prototype is a proof-of-concept; the LFP head is a simple MLP and the memory/segmentation heuristics are not learned end-to-end, limiting the strength of the paradigm-shift claims.
The surprise threshold requires tuning per video duration and per task, which is not a fully autonomous mechanism.
The paper does not evaluate failure cases or provide error analysis on VSI-Super, making it difficult to understand whether failures stem from perception, memory, or reasoning.

Potential domain leakage: VSI-590K is built from the same ScanNet/ScanNet++/ARKitScenes families that underlie VSI-Bench and hence VSI-Super; although the paper states train/test splits do not overlap, the model may still benefit from shared scene statistics, which weakens the claim of generalization to unseen spatial environments.
Potential negative societal impacts of 'supersensing' or surveillance applications are not discussed.
Computational costs of training the Cambrian-S family on TPU v4-512s are not quantified, which makes it harder for the community to replicate or assess the environmental impact.

final_review.Summary: The paper argues that progress toward 'spatial supersensing' requires moving beyond language-centric and reactive video understanding toward continuous, predictive world modeling. It proposes a four-stage hierarchy (semantic perception, streaming event cognition, implicit 3D spatial cognition, predictive world modeling), introduces a new benchmark VSI-Super with two tasks (VSR for long-horizon spatial recall and VSC for continual counting), and curates a large instruction-tuning dataset VSI-590K to train Cambrian-S models. Cambrian-S achieves large gains on VSI-Bench but still fails on VSI-Super, motivating a predictive-sensing prototype that uses latent-frame prediction error ('surprise') to drive memory management and event segmentation, improving performance on VSI-Super over strong baselines.
Strengths: The paper provides a thoughtful capability hierarchy for spatial supersensing and uses it to audit existing benchmarks, showing that many video benchmarks are solvable from captions or single frames and thus rely more on language priors than genuine visual sensing.

VSI-Super is a creative benchmark design: VSR resembles a visual needle-in-a-haystack with in-frame edited objects and sequential recall, while VSC requires continual counting across concatenated scenes; both are deliberately resistant to context-length scaling.

The curation of VSI-590K from diverse real, simulated, and pseudo-annotated sources is technically sound, and the data-source ablations are informative (annotated real videos > simulated > pseudo-annotated images).
Cambrian-S obtains a large +30% absolute improvement on VSI-Bench over prior open models without sacrificing general video understanding, and this holds across model sizes from 0.5B to 7B.

The predictive-sensing proof-of-concept is a distinctive contribution: using next-latent-frame prediction error as a surprise signal for memory compression and event segmentation yields consistent gains on VSI-Super and stable GPU memory use, outperforming Gemini-2.5-Flash and existing long-video methods.
The paper is generally well structured and includes extensive ablations, training details, and benchmark construction details in the appendices.
Weaknesses: The VSI-Super benchmark is synthetic and somewhat narrow: VSR is constructed by inserting out-of-place objects and concatenating room-tour videos, and VSC concatenates VSI-Bench clips; it is unclear how well these tasks capture real-world continuous spatial cognition or generalize beyond indoor tours.

The absolute performance of the proposed predictive-sensing system remains low (e.g., VSR around 40% and VSC around 35-40%), and the claimed superiority over Gemini-2.5-Flash is demonstrated on only these two synthetic tasks with a limited set of baselines.

The surprise threshold appears to be tuned per video duration and per method, which weakens the claim of a general, unsupervised mechanism; no analysis is provided on sensitivity to this hyperparameter or on how to set it in practice without ground-truth boundaries.

The comparison to 'streaming' models such as Gemini-Live and GPT-Realtime is limited to a figure with no detailed evaluation protocol or error bars, and these APIs may not be optimized for the exact counting task.

The paper frames 'supersensing' and 'predictive world modeling' as a paradigm shift, but the actual contribution is a lightweight MLP predictor plus heuristic memory/segmentation rules; the gap between the conceptual claims and the implemented prototype is large.

No human performance baselines are reported on VSI-Super, despite the claim that the tasks are 'easy for humans'; this makes it hard to calibrate how far models are from human-level spatial supersensing.

The VSR questions are multiple-choice with only four options, which may introduce guessing-level performance and limits the diagnostic power; the benchmark report includes chance levels but not per-question confidence or error analysis.
Questions: How sensitive are VSR and VSC results to the surprise threshold, and is it possible to set this threshold without knowing ground-truth event boundaries or video statistics?
Do the reported VSC streaming results control for the fact that the same question is asked repeatedly, possibly allowing models to accumulate answers or exploit repetition?
What is the human performance on VSI-Super, and how do the proposed methods compare to humans in terms of accuracy and robustness?
Does the predictive-sensing memory system work on more diverse, non-indoor, or real-world streaming videos, and does the LFP head generalize beyond the indoor room-tour distribution?

How much of the VSI-Super gain comes from the surprise-based memory/segmentation versus the underlying strong Cambrian-S spatial model trained on VSI-590K? A model with random or uniform segmentation would help isolate this.

Were the Gemini-2.5-Flash and other API baselines given any task-specific prompting or few-shot examples, and are their context windows actually exhausted at the stated video lengths given 1 FPS sampling?
How is the mean relative accuracy (MRA) computed for VSC exactly, and how are repeated observations of the same object across concatenated rooms handled in the ground-truth counts?
For VSR, are the inserted objects always placed in four locations chosen by human annotators, and if so, what is the inter-annotator agreement or quality control for the benchmark labels?
In the predictive sensing experiments, are the surprise thresholds tuned on the test set or on a separate validation set, and could threshold tuning per duration inflate the reported results?

Could a simple scene-change detector or optical-flow-based surprise signal combined with the same memory/segmentation framework match or exceed the LFP-based results? The current ablation only compares against adjacent-frame SigLIP similarity.

How does Cambrian-S with surprise memory perform on VSI-Super videos created from scenes outside the ScanNet/ARKitScenes/ScanNet++ distribution (e.g., outdoors, dynamic scenes, or other indoor datasets)?

Why does Cambrian-S without memory obtain only 0.6 MRA on 10-minute VSC despite strong absolute counting on VSI-Bench? Does this indicate a failure in cumulative state tracking rather than spatial perception?
Are the VSI-Super evaluation sets large enough for the reported differences (e.g., 60 VSR videos and 50 VSC questions per cell) to be statistically reliable?
Limitations: VSI-Super is synthetic and limited to indoor environments and concatenated room-tour clips, so its conclusions may not transfer to diverse real-world streaming scenarios.

The benchmark tasks are narrow (object recall and counting) and do not cover the full breadth of the proposed 'supersensing' hierarchy, particularly predictive world modeling or implicit 3D spatial cognition.

The predictive-sensing prototype is a proof-of-concept; the LFP head is a simple MLP and the memory/segmentation heuristics are not learned end-to-end, limiting the strength of the paradigm-shift claims.
The surprise threshold requires tuning per video duration and per task, which is not a fully autonomous mechanism.
The paper does not evaluate failure cases or provide error analysis on VSI-Super, making it difficult to understand whether failures stem from perception, memory, or reasoning.

Potential domain leakage: VSI-590K is built from the same ScanNet/ScanNet++/ARKitScenes families that underlie VSI-Bench and hence VSI-Super; although the paper states train/test splits do not overlap, the model may still benefit from shared scene statistics, which weakens the claim of generalization to unseen spatial environments.
Potential negative societal impacts of 'supersensing' or surveillance applications are not discussed.
Computational costs of training the Cambrian-S family on TPU v4-512s are not quantified, which makes it harder for the community to replicate or assess the environmental impact.
